source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The drugs have opposing cardiac effects, so combining them generally prevents bradycardia and atrioventricular conduction delay.","B":"Only the beta-blocker slows cardiac conduction, while verapamil primarily increases heart rate through peripheral vasodilation.","C":"Both drugs can slow heart rate and atrioventricular conduction, increasing the clinical risk of marked bradycardia or heart block.","D":"Both drugs primarily increase myocardial contractility, so the principal concern is severe tachycardia rather than bradycardia or heart block."}}
source_row.rationale: Both beta-blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (such as verapamil or diltiazem) can independently slow heart rate and cardiac conduction. Combining them significantly increases the risk of severe bradycardia, heart block, or worsened heart failure, so this combination requires careful monitoring and is often avoided or used with significant caution.
